blocks.text: Greece and Egypt can feel like two separate holidays joined into one. The first part might take you from the Acropolis in Athens to a few days on Santorini or Mykonos. Then a flight to Cairo changes the trip completely, with the Pyramids of Giza and, if you have enough time, Luxor, Aswan, and the Nile still ahead.

Our Greece & Egypt Tours range from 7 to 14 days. Shorter itineraries concentrate on Athens and Cairo, while additional days can be used for the Greek Islands, more of Egypt, or a combination of both.

Depending on the tour, arrangements can include hotels, guided sightseeing with local guides, airport and port transfers, regional and domestic flights, Greek ferry connections, and a Nile Cruise where specified. Private Tours and Customized Tours are available on selected itineraries.
Greece & Egypt Trip Planning • Local Teams in Both Countries • Island Flights & Ferries Coordinated • Cairo & Upper Egypt Arrangements • Nile Cruise Options • Support Across the Journey
With around 7 days, keeping to Athens and Cairo makes sense. Both cities have enough to see without using a large part of a short trip on additional flights and ferry connections.

Around 9 to 10 days gives you a choice. Those extra days can go toward Santorini and Mykonos, Alexandria, or additional time in Egypt. Two tours of the same length can therefore feel completely different.
At 11 to 14 days, combining the Greek Islands with more of Egypt becomes much more practical. Longer routes can move beyond Cairo to Luxor and Aswan, with a Nile Cruise included on selected programs.
More days give you options, but they do not need to mean more stops. An extra night on Santorini or along the Nile can sometimes improve the trip more than another destination.
This is the decision that shapes most Greece and Egypt itineraries.

If Santorini and Mykonos are high on your list, you need enough time in Greece to stay on the islands rather than simply pass through them. Athens plus one or two islands can easily take up a substantial part of the trip.
Egypt presents a different choice. Cairo and the Pyramids can be included in a shorter itinerary, but Luxor, Aswan, and a Nile Cruise need additional days.
With limited time, trying to include two Greek islands and the full Nile route usually means compromising somewhere. Decide which experience matters more before adding stops.

sections.heading: Getting from the Aegean to Cairo

blocks.text: Greece and Egypt are normally connected by air, with Athens and Cairo serving as the main gateways.

If your Greece itinerary includes Santorini or Mykonos, ferries or domestic flights are used to connect the islands with Athens or with each other, depending on the route and season. The international flight to Egypt is then arranged around the end of the Greece portion.

Once in Egypt, Cairo forms the starting point. Longer itineraries use domestic flights and ground transportation to continue into Upper Egypt, where a Nile Cruise can connect sightseeing between Luxor and Aswan.
This is a trip with several different types of transportation, so the order of the route matters as much as the places included.

sections.heading: What Changes When You Reach Egypt?

blocks.text: The pace of the journey changes.

Greek island itineraries usually leave room for independent time between transfers and sightseeing. Egypt tends to be more structured, particularly once the journey moves into Upper Egypt, where temple visits, domestic flights, transfers, and Nile Cruise schedules need to work together.
That difference can actually make the combination work well. A few slower days in Greece can sit comfortably alongside a more sightseeing-focused Egypt itinerary.
It is worth keeping that balance when choosing a tour rather than filling every available day with another excursion.

sections.heading: Greece & Egypt Tours at a Glance

rows: Santorini • Mykonos • Luxor • Aswan • Nile Cruise

blocks.text: Spring and autumn give the easiest overall balance between the two countries. March through May and September through November generally work well for sightseeing in Athens and Egypt while still fitting much of the Greek island season.
June through August is a natural choice when Santorini or Mykonos is the priority, but Egypt will be considerably hotter, particularly in Luxor and Aswan.

Winter works very well for Egypt, but it changes the Greece side of the trip. Island ferry schedules and seasonal tourism services are more limited, so a winter itinerary may make more sense with greater emphasis on Athens and Egypt.
Start by deciding what you want the middle of the trip to look like.

If the Greek Islands are essential, give them enough nights and keep the Egypt section more focused when necessary. If seeing Luxor, Aswan, and travelling on the Nile matters more, use those additional days in Egypt rather than trying to fit every island into the same itinerary.
With enough time, you do not have to choose: longer Greece & Egypt Tours can include Athens, the islands, Cairo, and the Nile in the same journey.
For an itinerary that also includes Turkey, see our Turkey, Greece & Egypt Tours. If you would rather travel in one country only, compare our Greece Tours or Egypt Tours.

faqs.q: What are the highlights of a Greece and Egypt combined tour?
faqs.a: In Greece: Acropolis with the Parthenon in Athens, caldera views at Oia in Santorini, a caldera boat cruise, and the Akrotiri Bronze Age excavation. In Egypt: Great Pyramid and Sphinx at Giza, Grand Egyptian Museum with the complete Tutankhamun collection, Karnak Temple in Luxor, Valley of the Kings, and a 3 to 4-day Nile cruise to Aswan.

faqs.q: How many days do I need for Greece and Egypt?
faqs.a: Ten days covers Athens, Santorini, Cairo, and a Nile cruise without feeling rushed. Twelve days adds Mykonos or Abu Simbel. Fourteen days is recommended for first-time visitors who want 2 to 3 days in each main location.

faqs.q: How much does a Greece and Egypt combined tour cost in 2026?
faqs.a: Ten-day Small group tours cost approximately 2,100 to 2,900 USD per person. Twelve to fourteen-day packages cost 2,700 to 4,000 USD per person. Contact us for a current quote.

faqs.q: Is the flight from Athens to Cairo included?
faqs.a: Yes. The international flight from Athens to Cairo is included. Your flight from your home country to Athens and the return from Cairo are not included.

faqs.q: Do I need visas for both Greece and Egypt?
faqs.a: Greece (Schengen) requires no visa for US, UK, Canadian, and Australian citizens for stays under 90 days. Egypt requires a visa; e-Visa at visa2egypt.gov.eg for approximately 25 USD, or visa on arrival at Cairo airport

faqs.q: Is the Nile cruise included in Greece and Egypt packages?
faqs.a: On packages of 10 days or more that cover the Luxor and Aswan section, yes. The standard Nile cruise runs 3 to 4 days from Luxor to Aswan with full board, Egyptologist guide, and shore excursion entrance fees.

faqs.q: Is an archaeologist guide included for the Acropolis?
faqs.a: Yes. Greek law requires licensed guides at all archaeological sites. A licensed archaeologist guide leads the Acropolis visit, typically 2 to 3 hours covering the Parthenon, Erechtheion, Propylaea, and Temple of Athena Nike.

faqs.q: Are Egyptologist guides included in Egypt?
faqs.a: Yes. All Egypt portions use licensed Egyptologist guides who hold degrees in Egyptology or archaeology. Licensed guides are required by Egyptian law at all major archaeological sites.

faqs.q: Can I add Greek island hopping?
faqs.a: Yes. Mykonos, Crete, or Rhodes can be added after Santorini on private tours. Island extensions require 12 to 14 days minimum to include meaningful time in Egypt. All ferry and internal flight connections are arranged and included.

faqs.q: Can Greece and Egypt be extended to include Turkey?
faqs.a: Yes. Turkey, Greece, and Egypt combined tour adds Istanbul and Cappadocia before the Greece portion, running 16 to 19 days total.
